Under ordinary conditions, elemental mercury cannot be a solid at room temperature; it is a freely-flowing liquid, as its freezing point is approximately -39°C [d2][d3][d8]. Multiple sources confirm this: mercury stays liquid until its temperature drops to around -40°C [d6], and at room temperature it exists in liquid form, freezing only at -38.8°C [d5]. However, mercury can exist as a solid in compound forms — for example, as a solid crystal salt or in the mineral cinnabar found in nature [d4][d7]. Even under specialized nanoscale experimental conditions, solidification of mercury does not occur at room temperature, beginning only at around 205 K during cooling [d1].
